properties.description: Respawns all players and ghosts on their respective starting squares based on spawn types.

If the spawn type is Ghost, it retrieves the next ghost from the npcs iterator and calls occupy(square). An index tracks player placement while an iterator tracks ghost placement.

The npcs map is non-null and contains at least as many ghosts as there are Ghost spawn squares.
The ghostIterator is derived from npcs.keySet() and will have enough elements.

properties.description: This package implements the ghost non-player characters (NPCs) in the Pac-Man game, encapsulating their unique AI behaviors and movement patterns. This package contains the core domain logic for the PacMan game, implementing fundamental game mechanics and rules. It manages game entities including Player, Pellet, and Ghost units, handles collision detection and resolution through a flexible handler system, and controls level state transitions. The package provides parsing capabilities to create levels from map representations and uses factories to instantiate game objects. It also implements an observer pattern for level events (won, lost, respawn) and coordinates NPC movement through scheduled tasks. All classes focus exclusively on game rules, entity behaviors, and state management without any UI, persistence, or external integration concerns.

properties.docComment:
{@inheritDoc }

Inky has the most complicated AI of all. Inky considers two things: Blinky's location, and the location two grid spaces ahead of Pac-Man. Inky draws a line from Blinky to the spot that is two squares in front of Pac-Man and extends that line twice as far. Therefore, if Inky is alongside Blinky when they are behind Pac-Man, Inky will usually follow Blinky the whole time. But if Inky is in front of Pac-Man when Blinky is far behind him, Inky tends to want to move away from Pac-Man (in reality, to a point very far ahead of Pac-Man). Inky is affected by a similar targeting bug that affects Speedy. When Pac-Man is moving or facing up, the spot Inky uses to draw the line is two squares above and left of Pac-Man.

Implementation: To actually implement this in jpacman we have the following approximation: first determine the square of Blinky (A) and the square 2 squares away from Pac-Man (B). Then determine the shortest path from A to B regardless of terrain and walk that same path from B. This is the destination.
properties.description: Calculate the next AI move for Inky ghost based on Blinky's position and player's predicted location.
properties.howItWorks: The method first locates the nearest Blinky and player units using BFS. It then calculates the player's future position after a fixed look-ahead distance. A path from Blinky to that future position is computed and followed to determine an intermediate destination. Finally, a path from Inky's current position to that destination is calculated, and the first direction of that path is returned if available.

properties.docComment:
An implementation of the classic Pac-Man ghost Inky.

AI: Inky has the most complicated AI of all. Inky considers two things: Blinky's location, and the location two grid spaces ahead of Pac-Man. Inky draws a line from Blinky to the spot that is two squares in front of Pac-Man and extends that line twice as far. Therefore, if Inky is alongside Blinky when they are behind Pac-Man, Inky will usually follow Blinky the whole time. But if Inky is in front of Pac-Man when Blinky is far behind him, Inky tends to want to move away from Pac-Man (in reality, to a point very far ahead of Pac-Man). Inky is affected by a similar targeting bug that affects Speedy. When Pac-Man is moving or facing up, the spot Inky uses to draw the line is two squares above and left of Pac-Man.

Source: http://strategywiki.org/wiki/Pac-Man/Getting_Started

When the ghosts are not patrolling in their home corners (Blinky: top-right, Pinky: top-left, Inky: bottom-right, Clyde: bottom-left), Blinky will attempt to shorten the distance between Pac-Man and himself. If he has to choose between shortening the horizontal or vertical distance, he will choose to shorten whichever is greatest. For example, if Pac-Man is four grid spaces to the left, and seven grid spaces above Blinky, he'll try to move up towards Pac-Man before he moves to the left.

If a valid path exists, it returns the first direction as an Optional; otherwise, it returns an empty Optional.

It requires no parameters and returns an Optional Direction that the game uses to move the ghost. The method handles all AI logic internally based on the current board state.

properties.docComment:
An implementation of the classic Pac-Man ghost Clyde.

Pokey needs a new nickname because out of all the ghosts, Clyde is the least likely to "C'lyde" with Pac-Man. Clyde is always the last ghost out of the regenerator, and the loner of the gang, usually off doing his own thing when not patrolling the bottom-left corner of the maze. His behavior is very random, so while he's not likely to be following you in hot pursuit with the other ghosts, he is a little less predictable, and still a danger.

AI: Clyde has two basic AIs, one for when he's far from Pac-Man, and one for when he is near to Pac-Man. When Clyde is far away from Pac-Man (beyond eight grid spaces), Clyde behaves very much like Blinky, trying to move to Pac-Man's exact location. However, when Clyde gets within eight grid spaces of Pac-Man, he automatically changes his behavior and runs away.

Source: http://strategywiki.org/wiki/Pac-Man/Getting_Started

@author Jeroen Roosen
properties.description: Clyde is a specific ghost NPC in Pac-Man with unique AI behavior. It extends the Ghost base class and implements a shyness mechanic where the ghost runs away from Pac-Man when within 8 grid spaces but chases when farther away. The class uses pathfinding to determine optimal movement and includes timing constants for movement intervals.
properties.secdfdEvidence: The nextAiMove() method performs non-trivial computation including player location search, shortest path calculation, and conditional logic based on distance threshold, representing a computational process that transforms game state into movement decisions.

properties.docComment:
{@inheritDoc }

When the ghosts are not patrolling their home corners, Pinky wants to go to the place that is four grid spaces ahead of Pac-Man in the direction that Pac-Man is facing. If Pac-Man is facing down, Pinky wants to go to the location exactly four spaces below Pac-Man. Moving towards this place uses the same logic that Blinky uses to find Pac-Man's exact location. Pinky is affected by a targeting bug if Pac-Man is facing up - when he moves or faces up, Pinky tries moving towards a point up, and left, four spaces.
properties.description: Calculates the next AI move for the Pinky ghost by targeting a square ahead of the nearest player and returning the first direction of the shortest path.
properties.howItWorks: The method asserts the ghost has a square, finds the nearest player using Navigation.findNearest, calculates a destination square four steps ahead of the player using squaresAheadOf, computes the shortest path from the ghost to that destination using Navigation.shortestPath, and returns the first direction if a non-empty path exists.
properties.howToUse: This method is called by the game AI system to determine the ghost's movement direction. It returns an Optional containing the chosen Direction or an empty Optional if no valid move is available.
postConditions: Returns an Optional<Direction> that may contain a valid direction or be empty
If a path exists, the returned direction is the first step towards the target square
The ghost's state is not modified by this method
preConditions: The ghost must be currently located on a square (hasSquare() == true)
The player must exist and be reachable on the board

properties.docComment:
An implementation of the classic Pac-Man ghost Shadow.

Nickname: Blinky. As his name implies, Shadow is usually a constant shadow on Pac-Man's tail. When he's not patrolling the top-right corner of the maze, Shadow tries to find the quickest route to Pac-Man's position. Despite the fact that Pinky's real name is Speedy, Shadow is actually the fastest of the ghosts because of when there are only a few pellets left, Blinky drastically speeds up, which can make him quite deadly. In the original Japanese version, his name is Oikake/Akabei.

AI: When the ghosts are not patrolling in their home corners (Blinky: top-right, Pinky: top-left, Inky: bottom-right, Clyde: bottom-left), Blinky will attempt to shorten the distance between Pac-Man and himself. If he has to choose between shortening the horizontal or vertical distance, he will choose to shorten whichever is greatest. For example, if Pac-Man is four grid spaces to the left, and seven grid spaces above Blinky, he'll try to move up towards Pac-Man before he moves to the left.

Source: http://strategywiki.org/wiki/Pac-Man/Getting_Started

@author Jeroen Roosen
properties.description: Blinky is a concrete ghost NPC in the PacMan game that implements specific AI behavior to chase the player by calculating the shortest path. properties.docComment:
{@inheritDoc }

Clyde has two basic AIs, one for when he's far from Pac-Man, and one for when he is near to Pac-Man. When Clyde is far away from Pac-Man (beyond eight grid spaces), Clyde behaves very much like Blinky, trying to move to Pac-Man's exact location. However, when Clyde gets within eight grid spaces of Pac-Man, he automatically changes his behavior and runs away
properties.description: Calculates the next movement direction for the Clyde ghost based on proximity to the player and pathfinding.
properties.howItWorks: The method first locates the nearest player using breadth-first search via Navigation.findNearest(). It then computes the shortest path to that player using Navigation.shortestPath(). If a valid path exists, it examines the path length: if the path size is less than or equal to Clyde's SHYNESS constant, the ghost moves in the opposite direction (shy behavior); otherwise it follows the first step of the path. If no player is found or no path exists, it returns an empty Optional.
properties.howToUse: This method is invoked by the game loop to determine Clyde's next move. It returns an Optional containing the chosen Direction, or an empty Optional if no valid move is available. No parameters are required; the method uses the ghost's current position and board state.
postConditions: Returns an Optional that may contain a Direction or be empty
Does not modify the ghost's position
preConditions: The ghost must be on a square (hasSquare() returns true)
The board must be properly initialized
properties.returns: An Optional containing the Direction Clyde should move next, or empty if no move is possible.
properties.secdfdEvidence: The method performs non-trivial computation: it searches for the nearest player, calculates a shortest path, and applies conditional logic based on path length and ghost-specific shyness threshold. It transforms input state (current position, board layout) into an output decision (next direction).

properties.docComment:
An implementation of the classic Pac-Man ghost Speedy.

Nickname: Pinky. Speedy gets his name for an unusual reason. Speedy appears to try to outsmart Pac-Man and crash into Pac-Man from the opposite direction. The truth behind this is that when Speedy isn't patrolling the top-left corner of the maze, he tries to attack Pac-Man by moving to where he is going to be (that is, a few spaces ahead of Pac-Man's current direction) instead of right where he is, as Blinky does. It's difficult to use this to your advantage, but it's possible. If Pinky is coming at you and you face a different direction, even briefly, he may just turn away and attempt to cut you off in the new direction while you return to your original direction. In the original Japanese version, his name is Machibuse/Pinky.

AI: When the ghosts are not patrolling their home corners, Pinky wants to go to the place that is four grid spaces ahead of Pac-Man in the direction that Pac-Man is facing. If Pac-Man is facing down, Pinky wants to go to the location exactly four spaces below Pac-Man. Moving towards this place uses the same logic that Blinky uses to find Pac-Man's exact location. Pinky is affected by a targeting bug if Pac-Man is facing up - when he moves or faces up, Pinky tries moving towards a point up, and left, four spaces.

Note: In the original arcade series, the ghosts' genders are unspecified and assumed to be male. In 1999, the USA division of Namco and Namco Hometech developed the Pac-Man World series and declared Pinky to be female.

Source: http://strategywiki.org/wiki/Pac-Man/Getting_Started

@author Jeroen Roosen

The Player class represents a core game entity with business logic (health management, scoring, death handling) and is independent of UI, data persistence, or service orchestration. It belongs to the domain model of the PacMan game.
The Player class primarily encapsulates state (health, score, alive, etc.) and provides accessor methods, while also containing some domain-specific behavior like damage handling and scoring.

The Player class holds valuable game state (health, score, alive status) that has business significance in the game. It is a data object that could be targeted for security considerations (e.g., cheating, integrity).

The Wall class represents a core business concept (a wall in the PacMan game) with domain-specific rules (inaccessibility). It contains no UI logic, service orchestration, or data persistence code, making it a pure domain model element.

The Wall class primarily holds the background Sprite data and provides access to it via getSprite(), while its accessibility behavior is a simple rule; its main responsibility is to encapsulate the visual and functional properties of a wall cell.

The Wall class is a domain entity that represents a valuable game element (a wall cell) with both visual (Sprite) and behavioral (accessibility) properties. It is part of the game's core state and has business value within the game mechanics.

Ground is part of the domain model representing a core game concept (a board tile) with domain-specific rules (always accessible), placing it in the Domain Layer rather than Presentation, Service, or Data Source layers.

Ground primarily stores data (sprite, spawn type) and provides simple accessor methods, with minimal behavior beyond returning a constant accessibility value, fitting the Information Holder stereotype.

The class is a simple domain object with a sprite field and a constant-return method; it does not perform non-trivial computation, store data persistently, interact with external entities, or represent a security-sensitive asset, so its SecDFD classification is undetermined.

The Game class encapsulates fundamental business logic and rules of the PacMan game (e.g., when a game can start, how it ends, how player moves affect score). It directly manipulates domain entities (Level, Player) and does not depend on or expose any UI or data access concerns, placing it squarely in the domain layer.

The Game class makes core decisions about game flow (start, stop, respawn), validates preconditions (players alive, pellets remaining), and orchestrates interactions between Level, Player, and PointCalculator components, acting as the central authority for game state transitions.

The Game class performs non-trivial orchestration logic: it coordinates multiple domain objects (Level, PointCalculator, Player), enforces game rules (checking inProgress, player alive status, pellet existence), and manages state transitions. It acts as a process that transforms input (player move commands, level events) into state changes and outputs (score updates, level resets).

It's in the Presentation Layer because it deals exclusively with visual assets used for rendering the game interface. It has no business logic, data persistence, or service orchestration responsibilities. It provides the graphical resources that the rendering system consumes.

It's a Service Provider because it implements specific sprite-related services (loading, animation creation, retrieval) and is invoked by other components to obtain sprite resources. It's not merely a data holder as it contains significant logic for processing sprite sheets and managing animations.

This class handles fundamental game mechanics (collision outcomes, scoring, state changes) which are part of the domain's business rules. It doesn't deal with presentation, data access, or application orchestration, placing it squarely in the domain layer.
The class implements a well-defined interface (CollisionMap) with a focused responsibility of handling collisions, making it a classic service provider that encapsulates collision logic.

The class contains methods that implement collision logic with conditional branching (instanceof checks), state modifications (pellet.leaveSquare(), player damage), and coordination with a PointCalculator, representing a process that transforms game state.
It encapsulates core game mechanics (collision logic) which is part of the business domain of PacMan, without concerns for UI, persistence, or external systems.
It primarily manages a nested map structure that organizes collision handlers by unit class pairs, acting as a registry for collision interactions.

The class performs active computation by dispatching collision events to registered handlers and managing the handler registry, which involves processing input (collision events) to produce game state changes.
It encapsulates core game mechanics and business logic for collision resolution, which is fundamental to the PacMan domain. It doesn't concern itself with UI, data persistence, or external systems.
It implements the CollisionMap interface and provides a specific collision handling service for player-related interactions.

The class performs non-trivial computation by delegating collision events to configured handlers that modify game state (player death, point awards, pellet removal). It orchestrates collision resolution logic specific to player interactions.

This class implements core game logic for handling collisions between units in the PacMan game. It directly manipulates game state through delegated collision processing and is concerned with business rules rather than presentation, data persistence, or service orchestration.

It implements the CollisionHandler interface and provides a specific collision handling service through a focused delegation pattern, acting as a strategy that modifies behavior by inverting argument order.

The class contains non-trivial computation logic that processes collisions by delegating to a wrapped handler with reversed parameters, representing a processing step in the collision management system that modifies game state.
ImageSprite deals directly with graphical rendering using java.awt.Graphics and image manipulation, which are core responsibilities of the Presentation Layer for UI/visual display.
ImageSprite implements the Sprite interface and provides concrete services for drawing, splitting, and querying image dimensions, acting as a provider of visual representation functionality.

ImageSprite encapsulates a graphical asset (java.awt.Image) that holds business/value as a visual element in the game; it does not perform orchestration, persist data, or interact with external systems.

EmptySprite deals directly with graphics rendering and visual elements, belonging to the Presentation Layer which manages UI and display concerns. It does not contain business logic, data access, or orchestration.
EmptySprite implements the Sprite interface, providing a concrete (though empty) implementation that handles rendering requests with a no-op strategy, fitting the Service Provider stereotype.
EmptySprite is a concrete class representing a visual element (sprite) that could be considered an asset in the game's resource system, though it holds no actual image data.

The class directly handles visual rendering and animation, which are core concerns of the user interface. It does not contain business logic, data access, or orchestration, but focuses on how sprites are displayed and animated on screen.
AnimatedSprite implements the Sprite interface and provides the service of rendering an animated sequence, encapsulating animation logic and frame management.

The class contains active logic for updating animation frames based on elapsed time, managing animation state (start/stop/restart), and delegating drawing operations, representing a processing unit that transforms state and performs rendering work.

This class encapsulates core business logic of the PacMan game (scoring rules) and operates on domain entities (Player, Pellet, Ghost). It has no concerns about UI, persistence, or external systems, focusing purely on the game mechanics and point calculation strategy.
The class implements a specific interface (PointCalculator) and provides concrete implementations for handling game events related to point calculation, serving as a strategy for scoring in the game.

The class contains non-trivial computation logic (adding points based on pellet values) and orchestrates responses to game events by modifying domain state (player scores), representing a process in the data flow diagram.

Inky encapsulates core game logic and business rules for ghost behavior, directly representing a domain concept (a ghost with specific AI) in the PacMan game. It does not handle UI, service orchestration, or data persistence, which are responsibilities of other layers.
Inky's primary responsibility is to make decisions about its movement direction based on the game state, controlling its behavior as an autonomous agent in the game.

Inky performs non-trivial computation to determine its movement, involving BFS searches, path calculations, and AI targeting logic that orchestrates multiple game entities (Blinky, player) to produce a decision.

Pinky implements domain-specific AI behavior for a game entity, containing business rules (targeting 4 squares ahead) and computations (pathfinding), which are characteristic of the domain layer. It doesn't handle UI, data access, or orchestration across services.
Pinky encapsulates autonomous decision-making logic for its movement, determining its next direction based on player position and orientation.

The nextAiMove() method performs non-trivial computation: finding nearest player, calculating target position, computing shortest path, and returning a direction, representing a computational process that transforms game state data.
The class is part of the game's domain model, implementing NPC behavior and movement logic, which is core domain functionality rather than presentation, service orchestration, or data access.
The class overrides nextAiMove() to determine the next direction the ghost should move, effectively controlling its autonomous movement behavior.
The class overrides nextAiMove() to compute or determine the next movement direction, representing a processing step in the game's AI system.
Blinky represents a core game entity with specific business logic (ghost AI behavior) that is independent of UI, data persistence, or service orchestration.
Blinky makes autonomous decisions about its movement direction based on game state, controlling its own behavior as an NPC.

The nextAiMove() method performs non-trivial computation including finding the nearest player and calculating shortest paths, which represents a process that transforms data (board state) into a decision (movement direction).

The Clyde class resides in the domain layer as it encapsulates core game business logic specific to Pac-Man. It implements the unique behavioral rules for this ghost type (shyness threshold, chase/run-away logic) and performs domain computations like distance calculation and pathfinding. It does not interact with UI, data persistence, or external services, focusing purely on domain behavior.

The Clyde class functions as a controller by making autonomous decisions about the ghost's movement direction based on game state (player proximity) and implementing specific control logic for this NPC's behavior.

The nextAiMove() method performs non-trivial computation including player location search, shortest path calculation, and conditional logic based on distance threshold, representing a computational process that transforms game state into movement decisions.
It encapsulates core business logic of the Pac-Man game, managing game state, player, and level interactions without concerns for UI or data persistence.
It acts as the central controller for a single-player game instance, managing game state and coordinating with the level and player.

The class performs active game logic operations such as initializing the game, registering the player, and providing access to game components, representing a non-trivial computation within the system.

This package resides in the Domain Layer because it implements the core business logic and game rules of the Pac-Man application. The ghost classes encapsulate specific AI algorithms, movement patterns, and targeting strategies that define how ghosts behave according to the game's design. The Navigation class provides pathfinding utilities that are fundamental to the domain's computational needs. None of these components handle user interface concerns, data persistence, or service orchestration, which are responsibilities of other layers.

This package contains the core business logic and data structures of the PacMan game. It defines fundamental domain concepts like the board, squares, units, and directions, along with their behaviors and relationships. It does not handle user interface (Presentation), application orchestration (Service), or external data access (Data Source), making it a pure domain layer implementation.

This package represents the core business logic and domain model of the PacMan game. It encapsulates game rules, entity behaviors (Player, Pellet, Ghost), collision handling, level management, and state transitions. The classes are focused on implementing the fundamental mechanics of the game without any concerns for user interface (Presentation), data persistence (Data Source), or application flow orchestration (Service). All operations are domain-centric: moving NPCs, resolving collisions, parsing maps, and notifying observers about game events—pure business logic that would remain unchanged even if the UI or data storage were swapped out.

This package encapsulates the core business logic of the game - how points are awarded to the player. The PointCalculator interface and its implementations represent domain concepts and rules. While the loader performs configuration-based instantiation, its purpose is to supply the appropriate domain service, not to manage application flow or presentation. It does not interact with external data sources or UI, making the Domain Layer the most appropriate classification.

This package resides in the Domain Layer because it contains the central business logic of the Pac-Man game, including state management, rule enforcement, and coordination of domain entities (Level, Player, PointCalculator). It does not handle user interface, data persistence, or external system integration, focusing purely on the core game mechanics and flow.

This package belongs in the Presentation Layer because it is solely responsible for visual rendering and UI representation. All classes focus on how game elements appear on screen: Sprite defines the contract for drawable objects, ImageSprite and AnimatedSprite provide concrete rendering implementations, SpriteStore manages image resources, and PacManSprites organizes game-specific visual assets. The package contains no business logic, data persistence, or application flow control - it purely handles the visual presentation of the game to the user.

All classes in this package are directly responsible for the user interface: they extend Swing components (JPanel, KeyListener), manage visual rendering of game elements, handle user input events, and compose the main application window. They do not contain business logic, orchestrate domain operations, or interact with data sources, which clearly places them in the Presentation Layer.

This package resides in the Domain Layer because it encapsulates the business logic and rules governing ghost behavior in the PacMan game. It defines domain entities (Ghost and its subclasses), implements AI strategies, and provides pathfinding algorithms—all core domain computations. It does not handle user interface, data persistence, or service orchestration, which are responsibilities of other layers.

The package contains sub-packages from multiple architectural layers: the domain layer (board, npc, level, points, game), the presentation layer (sprite, ui), and the service layer (Launcher orchestrates initialization). Since it aggregates components across layers, it does not exclusively belong to a single layer.

The nl.tudelft package is a top-level namespace that does not contain any classes or implement any functionality; it merely acts as a container for the nl.tudelft.jpacman sub-package, which spans multiple architectural layers (domain, presentation, service). Since the package itself has no behavioral responsibility, it cannot be assigned to a specific architectural layer.

The nl package is a pure namespace container with no implementation classes. It does not contain any code that handles user interface, business logic, data access, or service orchestration. Its sole purpose is organizational, providing a unique root for the project's package structure. Therefore, it does not fit into any specific architectural layer.
